headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Perineal and Genital Lacerations
headings.content: Perineal and genital lacerations are common soft tissue injuries that occur during childbirth, primarily in the second stage of labour as the fetus passes through the birth canal. A laceration refers to a tear in the skin, mucous membranes, and underlying muscles of the perineum, vagina, cervix, or labia, distinct from an episiotomy which is a surgical incision. For nursing and midwifery students in Nigeria, understanding these tears is crucial because unmanaged or poorly repaired lacerations can lead to significant postpartum hemorrhage, infection, chronic pain, and long-term pelvic floor dysfunction, such as urinary or fecal incontinence. These injuries can occur spontaneously due to rapid fetal descent, macrosomia, or operative vaginal deliveries like forceps or vacuum extraction. Midwives must possess the foundational knowledge to differentiate between spontaneous tears and surgical cuts, assess the extent of the damage accurately, and provide prompt, effective care to promote optimal maternal recovery and preserve anatomical integrity.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Female Perineum and Pelvic Floor
headings.content: A thorough understanding of the anatomy of the female perineum and pelvic floor is essential for accurate assessment, classification, and repair of birth trauma. The perineum is a diamond-shaped area located between the thighs, bounded anteriorly by the pubic symphysis, posteriorly by the coccyx, and laterally by the ischial tuberosities. It is divided into the urogenital triangle anteriorly and the anal triangle posteriorly. The pelvic floor is primarily formed by the levator ani muscle group—comprising the iliococcygeus, pubococcygeus, and puborectalis muscles—along with the coccygeus muscle. These structures provide vital support to the pelvic organs, maintain urinary and fecal continence, and assist during childbirth by guiding the fetal head. During crowning and delivery, these muscles stretch significantly and can be subjected to high tension. Superficial perineal muscles, such as the bulbospongiosus, transverse perineal muscles, and the external anal sphincter, are also frequently involved in tears. Recognizing these anatomical landmarks enables midwives to re-approximate tissues accurately during suturing, ensuring restoration of both anatomy and physiological function.

headings.title: Classification and Degrees of Perineal Tears
headings.content: Perineal tears are classified into four distinct degrees based on the depth and extent of tissue involvement, which dictates the appropriate management and repair technique. A first-degree tear involves only the perineal skin and vaginal mucous membrane, often requiring no sutures if bleeding is minimal and edges are well-apposed. A second-degree tear involves the skin, mucous membranes, and the fascia and muscles of the perineal body, but spares the anal sphincter complex; this requires layered suturing by a trained clinician. A third-degree tear extends through the skin, mucous membrane, and perineal muscles, and further involves the anal sphincter complex. It is sub-classified into 3a (less than 50% of external anal sphincter torn), 3b (greater than 50% torn), and 3c (both external and internal anal sphincters torn). Finally, a fourth-degree tear involves all structures of a third-degree tear plus the anal epithelium and rectal mucosa, exposing the lumen of the rectum. Third and fourth-degree tears are collectively known as Obstetric Anal Sphincter Injuries (OASIS) and typically require repair in an operating theatre under regional or general anesthesia to prevent long-term fecal incontinence and fistula formation.

headings.title: Etiology and Risk Factors During Labour
headings.content: Understanding the etiology and risk factors for perineal lacerations allows midwives to anticipate complications and employ preventative measures during labour. Risk factors can be maternal, fetal, or iatrogenic. Maternal factors include nulliparity (first-time mothers have tighter, less compliant tissues), precipitous or prolonged second stage of labour, operative vaginal deliveries (forceps or vacuum extraction), persistent occipitoposterior fetal position, and previous perineal trauma or scarring. Fetal factors primarily involve macrosomia (large birth weight, typically over 4,000 grams) and shoulder dystocia, which stretch the perineum beyond its physiological limits. Iatrogenic factors include unmanaged rapid crowning, inappropriate use of fundal pressure, and routine or poorly timed episiotomies that extend into severe tears. Midwives can mitigate some of these risks through techniques such as controlled delivery of the fetal head (using the hands-on or hands-poised technique), warm compresses applied to the perineum during the second stage, and perineal massage, which help relax and stretch the tissues safely.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnosis of Lacerations
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnosis of lacerations require a systematic, gentle, and thorough postpartum examination of the lower genital tract. Immediately following the delivery of the placenta, the midwife must explain the procedure to the mother, ensure adequate lighting, and position her in the dorsal lithotomy or left lateral position with proper exposure. Inspection must be comprehensive, involving the labia, clitoris, urethra, vagina, cervix, and perineum. Gentle separation of the labia and visualization using sterile gauze and a good light source help identify the exact origin, length, and depth of any bleeding sites or tears. The midwife must specifically check the integrity of the anal sphincter by performing a digital rectal examination if a third- or fourth-degree tear is suspected, feeling for the tone and continuity of the sphincter muscles. Accurate diagnosis prevents missed injuries, ensures the correct classification of the tear, and dictates whether the repair can be performed locally by the midwife or requires referral to a physician or obstetrician.

headings.title: Immediate Midwifery Management and Repair
headings.content: Immediate midwifery management and repair of lacerations focus on achieving hemostasis, restoring anatomical alignment, and minimizing infection risk. Before beginning, the midwife must ensure informed consent, effective pain relief (such as local infiltration with 1% or 2% lidocaine), and strict aseptic technique. First-degree tears that are not bleeding and have well-apposed edges may be left un-sutured to heal naturally. Second-degree tears and higher require careful suturing using absorbable synthetic sutures (such as polyglactin 910/Vicryl). The repair starts at the apex of the vaginal component, continuing continuously or interruptedly down to the vaginal ring, followed by the reconstruction of the perineal muscles using interrupted or continuous stitches, and finally closing the skin. For third- and fourth-degree tears (OASIS), the midwife must immediately notify a senior clinician or obstetrician, as these require specialized repair techniques in a sterile theatre setting, often involving overlap or end-to-end approximation of the internal and external anal sphincters. Post-repair, a rectal and vaginal check must be performed to ensure no suture has accidentally been placed through the rectal mucosa.

headings.title: Postoperative Care and Pain Management
headings.content: Postoperative care and pain management are vital components of nursing care designed to promote wound healing, prevent infection, and enhance maternal comfort following laceration repair. The perineal wound should be kept clean and dry; mothers are educated on perineal hygiene, including washing the area from front to back using clean water after every micturition or defecation, and changing maternity pads frequently. Pain management is tailored using the WHO analgesic ladder, typically starting with mild non-opioid analgesics like paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, provided there are no contraindications. Stool softeners or mild laxatives (like lactulose) are frequently prescribed to prevent constipation and hard stools, which can strain the newly repaired perineum, especially in patients with OASIS. Midwives must regularly inspect the perineum for signs of hematoma formation, excessive edema, or localized infection (such as foul discharge, redness, or dehiscence) and encourage early ambulation to promote venous return and prevent deep vein thrombosis.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Long-term Sequelae
headings.content: Potential complications and long-term sequelae of perineal and genital lacerations can significantly impact a woman's physical, psychological, and social well-being if not promptly recognized and managed. Short-term complications include severe postpartum hemorrhage, acute perineal pain, wound hematomas, localized cellulitis, and wound dehiscence (breakdown of the repair). Long-term sequelae encompass chronic pelvic pain, dyspareunia (painful sexual intercourse), rectovaginal fistula formation, and pelvic floor dysfunction leading to stress urinary incontinence or fecal and flatal incontinence. Women experiencing these complications may suffer from psychological distress, postpartum depression, and strained marital relationships. Midwives play a crucial role during postnatal visits by screening for these complications, providing empathetic counseling, referring patients to specialized physiotherapy or surgical services when necessary, and reassuring mothers regarding pelvic recovery.
